metric.why: Rack density is the variable forcing the industry rebuild. Above roughly 30 kW per rack, air cooling stops being sufficient and liquid cooling, heavier floors, and different power distribution follow.
metric.target: NVIDIA's rack-scale GPU systems are specified above 100 kW per rack, which is why liquid cooling moved from exotic to default in new AI builds.
metric.definition: The kilowatts delivered to and dissipated by a single rack. Traditional enterprise racks ran 5 to 15 kW; dense GPU training racks are specified at 40 to over 100 kW.

reading.body:
Power density per rack, measured in kilowatts delivered to and dissipated by a single rack, has moved from a traditional band of 5 to 15 kW toward 40 to over 100 kW for dense GPU training racks, with NVIDIA's rack-scale systems specified above 100 kW.

Above roughly 30 kW per rack, air cooling stops being sufficient, which is why liquid cooling moved from an exotic option to the default choice in new AI builds. That threshold is not a marketing claim, it is a physical limit on how much heat a fan-driven airflow system can remove from a cabinet-sized space, so it explains directly why the entire cooling industry retooled around AI-era rack densities rather than incrementally improving air handling.

Three related metrics sit alongside this one, PUE and DCiE, which measure whole-facility power overhead, and breaker-level load and peak draw, which measures actual circuit consumption rather than rack specification. Rack density is the input variable and those others are downstream measurements of what that density costs to run.
